This led to widespread 3-5 inches of snow in central and eastern MA, eastern CT, and RI. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 7 to 10 inches of snow fell with a narrow swath of 12-13 inches. Some of the highest reports included 13.6 inches in Beverly and 13 inches in Salisbury.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A blockbuster winter storm that impacted millions across the lower 48, bringing a combination of ice; sleet; snow; rain; and strong winds, brought widespread heavy snowfall accumulations to all of western Massachusetts from January 25-26th, 2026. ||An arctic blast made for dangerously cold conditions across western Massachusetts from January 23-24, creating a requisite cold airmass that supported snow as the primary precipitation type with this storm. The connection of the northern and southern stream flow regimes then steered a potent, Gulf-originating low pressure system to the northeast. Strong to anomalous low- to mid-level dynamics drove impressive moisture transport from the Gulf and western Atlantic in and across the region the morning of the impending storm, Sunday January 25th. Snow began Sunday morning, initially with a large dendritic growth zone courtesy of persistent arctic air being filtered into the region from northerly flow about a nearby surface high to the northeast. However, as the storm tracked closer, its associated warm nose modified the thermal profile and shrunk and lifted the dendritic growth zone into the mid and upper levels of the atmosphere by the afternoon. Snowfall rates that initially looked to reach up to 2-4 per hour within laterally translating snow bands therefore became limited to 1-2 per hour courtesy of the disconnect between the best low-level forcing and the dendritic growth zone. Still, a widespread 10-20 of snow fell across the region between Sunday, January 25th and Monday, January 26th. ||The Governor of Massachusetts, Maura Healey, declared a state of emergency prior to this event which authorized additional local resources as well as orders for travel restrictions. NWS Albany additionally received reports of numerous school and road closures in addition to traffic accidents across western Massachusetts. ||Key Impacts: state of emergency declarations, road closures, school closures, traffic accidents.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Zone average snowfall of 15.5 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Explosive cyclogenesis of a low pressure center off the Mid Atlantic coast brought a strong winter storm with blizzard conditions to central and eastern Massachusetts as well as Rhode Island on Monday. The storm tracked from east of the Carolinas to the 70w/40n benchmark bringing extreme snowfall rates of 2 to 4 inches per hour and winds gusting to hurricane force along the coast and 50 to 60 mph inland. The heaviest snow was centered over central Rhode Island and southeast Massachusetts where over 30 inches of snow fell. The highest amount for the storm was 37.9 inches at T.F. Green Airport in Rhode Island.  Snow tapered off Monday evening. There was some minor to moderate coastal flooding along the eastern Massachusetts coast but impact from coastal flooding was minimal. This was a record breaking storm in some aspects including state snowfall records for Rhode Island. The storm crippled movement across much of southern New England especially southeast Massachusetts and Rhode Island where plows could not keep up and some municipalities actually halted plowing for a time at the peak. The combination of heavy, wet snow and strong winds led to many power outages especially over southeast Massachusetts where some did not get power for 4+ days. Cape Cod was especially hard hit with power outages.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 24 to 32 inches of snow fell. Some of the highest reports were 32 inches in Dighton and 32 inches in Attleboro. Winds generally gusted 50 to 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system impacted western Massachusetts on the final day of March of 2026, bringing widespread rainfall and evening thunderstorms as its associated cold front tracked through the region. Over the course of the event, about 0.5 to 1.3 inches of rain fell across western Massachusetts with the heaviest rainfall rates occurring within thunderstorms that tracked just ahead of the boundary in the late evening. While most thunderstorms proved to be sub-severe in strength, an isolated storm did, per radar estimation, produce a severe-level wind gust which downed a tree in Lenox.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Local law enforcement relayed a report of a downed tree in Lenox.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system brought a period of strong winds, along with rain, to western Massachusetts on March 16-17, 2026. Winds started in the southerly direction before switching to the west behind the cold front. Widespread wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph were observed with localized gusts to around 55 mph. Approximately 300 customers lost power across Berkshire County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 55 mph wind gust was recorded at the Pittsfield Municipal Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Within the warm sector of a low pressure system, sufficient destabilization and increased shear ahead of a prefrontal trough led to the development of scattered showers and thunderstorms that tracked into western Massachusetts on April 14th. In the evening of April 14th, a cluster of thunderstorms morphed into more of a linear segment which produced severe wind gusts that led to reports of tree damage and subsequent traffic delays near Lee and Dalton, Massachusetts. Additionally, the Pittsfield ASOS recorded a peak wind gust of 59 mph when this storm moved over it.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Pittsfield ASOS measured a wind gust of 59 mph and reported it through an updated METAR at 658 PM.
